words.context: The greeting, usually compressed to two syllables. “Not bad, you?” closes it.
“Ta” is more common here than in London and isn’t casual — people use it with strangers.
“Ta-ra,” said tah-RAH, is the local version and still widely used. “Laters” among younger people.
Works for apologising and for getting past, the same reflex as the rest of England.
Bar service by eye contact and patience. Waving gets you nowhere and gets noticed.
Asking for “the check” marks you instantly.
Usually 10% and added mainly in city-center restaurants. Removable on request and stated on the bill.
Bee Network buses and trams take contactless with daily capping. Metrolink has no barriers but inspectors do check.
“Loo” works, “bogs” is cruder and common. “Restroom” gets a blank look.

words.groupNote: Standard on most doors. Pubs occasionally get creative with it.

words.context: Also “the hole in the wall.” Avoid the ones that charge a fee.
Contactless everywhere. Say it as you hold the card up.
Still useful in older pubs and at the markets, though card works almost everywhere.
Charged. Say “no thanks” if you brought one.
Excellent. “That’s mint” is high praise and has nothing whatsoever to do with the flavor.
Good, fine, reliable, agreed. Also describes a person — “he’s sound” is a genuine compliment.
A sibling, usually a younger brother. Nothing at all to do with your own children.
A soft bread roll. Calling it a “bap,” a “cob,” or a “bun” starts a real argument that has never been settled.
The narrow alley running between terraced houses. Every Manchester childhood involves at least one.
A cup of tea. “Fancy a brew” is the standard offer, and refusing it outright is faintly odd.
Very. “Dead good” means very good, which trips up almost every visitor at least once.
“Mad for it” — total enthusiasm, straight out of the early nineties and never fully retired.
